CAD 20,000 now or CAD 24,000 later? Compare the date before comparing the dollars

Use a discount-rate curve, common-date value bars, a present-value waterfall and a rate-and-wait matrix to examine an immediate versus deferred lump sum.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Put immediate cash and a later lump sum on the same date

Interactive planning lab

Present value of the later payment at the selected rate$20,732.1
Present-value difference: later payment minus cash now$732.1
Annual break-even comparison rate for these two amounts6.27%

Two mutually exclusive hypothetical single receipts: one at time zero, the other after the selected whole years. CAD cash flows use the same nominal basis and are entered after any independently assumed deductions; no tax is computed. The comparison rate is effective annually and constant, not an available investment return, required lending rate or risk-free quote. The future-value comparison assumes the immediate amount could compound at that rate until the later date without withdrawals. No actual investment is selected. Full and timely payment is assumed; credit risk, access restrictions, inflation, fees and changing rates are not quantified. Present value is a valuation today, not cash already available to pay a bill.

On this page

  1. Write two alternatives, rather than one combined balance
  2. Convert the later receipt into a value measured today
  3. A discount-rate curve shows which assumption changes the answer
  4. Moving both alternatives forward gives the same ordering
  5. Solve for the annual rate instead of dividing 20% by three

The central idea

A larger later payment is not directly comparable with cash today. Put both alternatives on one date, show the implied annual rate, and separately check payment reliability and access.

01

Write two alternatives, rather than one combined balance

The example offers one of two receipts: CAD 20,000 today or a single CAD 24,000 payment in three years. Receiving one means giving up the other. Adding them into CAD 44,000 of household resources would count an alternative that was never available alongside the first.

The nominal difference is CAD 4,000, or 20% of the immediate amount. That 20% covers the entire three-year wait. It is not a 20% annual return. The dates are part of the comparison, just as surely as the amounts.

The CFA Institute’s public time-value overview connects current values, future cash flows and implied returns. Here, the calculator applies those principles to a simple original example with one payment under each alternative.

02

Convert the later receipt into a value measured today

Let L be the later payment, r the effective annual comparison rate as a fraction, and n the number of years. The present value is PV = L ÷ (1+r)n. This discounts the later amount over the actual waiting period.

At the default 5% comparison rate, CAD 24,000 divided by 1.05³ equals approximately CAD 20,732.10. Compared with CAD 20,000 today, the present-value difference is about CAD 732.10 in favour of the later receipt under the stated assumptions.

That value is not a deposit already held in an account. It is today’s equivalent on the selected valuation basis. A household cannot send CAD 20,732.10 to pay an earlier bill merely because the calculator displays that present value.

03

A discount-rate curve shows which assumption changes the answer

The first chart recalculates the later receipt’s present value at rates from 0% to 20%. The immediate CAD 20,000 remains a horizontal comparison. At a zero rate, the later receipt has a present value equal to its CAD 24,000 nominal amount. As the rate rises, its present value falls.

The crossing is useful because it identifies the rate at which the two valuations are equal. Below that rate, the later receipt has the greater present value. Above it, the immediate cash has the greater present value. Those statements hold for these fixed amounts and dates with full payment assumed.

The selected rate needs a reason. It might represent an independently assessed opportunity cost on a consistent cash basis, but the calculator does not identify an available deposit, achievable investment return or appropriate risk premium. An uncertain investment forecast cannot be turned into a guaranteed alternative simply by entering its average return here.

04

Moving both alternatives forward gives the same ordering

The common-date bars perform the comparison at the end of year three instead of today. Compounding CAD 20,000 at 5% for three years gives CAD 23,152.50. The alternative later receipt is CAD 24,000, leaving a future-date difference of CAD 847.50.

The present-date difference was CAD 732.10, not CAD 847.50. The two figures use different dates. Multiplying the unrounded present-value difference by 1.05³ converts it into the future-date difference. It does not create an extra source of profit.

The bars assume the immediate receipt remains invested at the entered constant rate with no withdrawals. If the cash is used for living costs, the resulting future balance will differ. Actual spending may meet a real need, but it cannot simultaneously remain available to compound toward the later comparison.

05

Solve for the annual rate instead of dividing 20% by three

The break-even annual rate solves cash now × (1+r*)n = later cash. Rearranging gives r* = (later cash ÷ cash now)1/n − 1.

For CAD 20,000 and CAD 24,000 three years later, the result is approximately 6.26586% effective annually. Compounding at that rate for three years produces the full 20% cumulative increase. Dividing 20% by three gives a simple average of about 6.67%, which does not preserve the compounding equation.

The rate is implied by the two offered amounts and their timing. It is not a separately earned coupon or an assurance that anyone will pay it. The California Board of Equalization’s time-value summary explains compounding and discounting as opposite movements between dates. This example uses annual effective compounding consistently in both directions.

06

Keep the future amount fixed when testing a longer delay

The matrix changes the waiting time and the comparison rate while retaining the same two receipt amounts. Every cell reports the later receipt’s present value minus the cash-now alternative. A longer wait does not automatically earn a larger payment in this exercise.

At a positive rate, postponing the same future amount reduces its present value. At a zero rate, changing the wait leaves the present-value amount unchanged, although the actual availability date still moves. This separates the valuation calculation from the practical need to use money before it arrives.

The matrix has no probabilities attached to its cells. It does not forecast which date or rate will occur. It helps reveal whether a conclusion depends strongly on a short delay or a particular valuation rate.

07

A break-even rate can sit outside the plotted range

If the two nominal amounts are identical, their implied break-even rate is zero. If the later amount is smaller than the immediate amount, the implied rate is negative. A nonnegative comparison rate will then favour the immediate amount on this narrow valuation basis.

A very large later amount over a short period can imply a break-even rate above the graph’s 20% ceiling. The metric still reports the calculated rate, while the chart shows only its stated 0% to 20% range. No crossing inside the visible graph should be invented.

These mathematical controls help interpret the output without treating an unusual implied rate as evidence that a high-return product exists. The legal terms, payment source and reliability of an actual offer require their own evidence.

08

Bring the valuation back to the household’s required dates

A bill due in six months cannot be paid directly by a receipt arriving in three years. A positive present-value difference does not supply a bridge loan, change the bill’s due date or make the later promise transferable. The calculator includes none of those arrangements.

Compare the actual net receipts on the same tax and cost basis. The model does not calculate tax, fees, inflation or default losses. It also does not convert nominal future cash into inflation-adjusted purchasing power; adding such a comparison would require a consistent real-cash and real-rate calculation.

  1. Confirm which receipts are mutually exclusive and when each is usable.
  2. Put their amounts on a consistent net-cash basis.
  3. Document the reason for the comparison rate.
  4. Check both present-date and common future-date values.
  5. Review payment reliability and earlier cash obligations separately.

The result is a transparent valuation comparison. The choice still has to support the actual payment calendar and the terms of the available alternatives.
